text: A single number, like average delivery time is 39.6 minutes, hides how uncertain it is. A confidence interval turns the standard error into a range of plausible values for the population parameter — something like between 37.9 and 41.4 minutes. Reporting an estimate together with its interval is one of the most honest and useful habits in data work.

The recipe is: estimate, plus or minus a critical value, times the standard error. For a mean with an estimated spread, we use the t distribution with n minus 1 degrees of freedom. Sampling 40 deliveries from a population whose true mean is about 40: the sample mean is 39.62, standard error 0.863, and the critical t value for 95 percent confidence is 2.023.

Putting it together gives a 95 percent confidence interval of 37.87 to 41.37 minutes, and the true mean, 40.01, sits right inside it. scipy's stats.t.interval returns the same thing directly. The 0.975 in the critical value comes from splitting the remaining 5 percent into two tails of 2.5 percent each.

This is the most misunderstood idea in statistics. It does not mean there's a 95 percent probability the true mean lies in this particular interval — the true mean is fixed, either in or out. The 95 percent describes the procedure: if you repeated the sampling process many times and built an interval each time, about 95 percent of those intervals would capture the truth.

Checking this directly: building 2,000 separate 95 percent intervals from 2,000 separate samples, 94.75 percent of them actually contained the true mean. Any single interval is a hit or a miss — you simply cannot tell which one yours is.

A more confident interval must be wider, and a larger sample makes it narrower. Demanding 90 percent confidence gives a width of 2.91; 95 percent gives 3.49; 99 percent gives 4.68 — roughly a third more width than 95 percent. Nothing is free: you trade certainty for precision.

By sample size: n of 10 gives a width of 6.85; n of 40 gives 3.21; n of 160 gives 1.51; n of 640 gives 0.77. Each fourfold increase in n roughly halves the width, echoing the same square-root rule from the standard error lesson.

For a proportion, like 120 of 400 customers returning an order, use the normal approximation — a 30 percent return rate with a 95 percent interval of about 25.5 to 34.5 percent. This approximation works poorly when n is small or p is near 0 or 1; check options like the Wilson interval in statsmodels for those cases.

The t interval assumes roughly normal sampling behavior. With strongly skewed data and a small sample, coverage falls short — simulating a very skewed log-normal population with samples of just 15, only about 86 percent of the 95 percent intervals actually caught the mean. Larger samples, or the bootstrap in the next lesson, fix this. And remember: a confidence interval only covers random error — a biased sample gives a confidently wrong interval, no matter how narrow.

To recap: a confidence interval is estimate plus or minus critical value times standard error. The confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the method, not the probability for your one interval. Higher confidence and smaller samples widen it, and strong skew plus a small sample can break it entirely.
